findings.title: Eviction netgroup secret is drawn at load time and frozen into the saved executable
findings.our_ref: src/node/eviction.lisp:92 (also src/node/entropy.lisp:33, src/node/init.lisp:11-17, scripts/build-node-core.lisp:16-29, src/node/eviction.lisp:88-97 and :56-58)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/init.cpp:1642-1648 (FastRandomContext rng; CConnman(rng.rand64(), rng.rand64(), ...)); refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:4131-4141 (GetDeterministicRandomizer / CalculateKeyedNetGroup); refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:110 (RANDOMIZER_ID_NETGROUP)
findings.core_does: Core draws nSeed0/nSeed1 per PROCESS from a default-constructed FastRandomContext (OS-seeded ChaCha20) at AppInitMain, and derives nKeyedNetGroup as SipHash-2-4 keyed with those two 64-bit words. Every start of the same binary gets a different key, so an attacker cannot compute which netgroups the eviction pass will protect.
findings.we_do: *eviction-netgroup-secret* is a DEFVAR whose initform is (random most-positive-fixnum). A defvar initform is evaluated at LOAD time, which is before seed-global-random-state ever runs (init.lisp calls it at the head of init-node, and its own comment claims 'nothing draws from SBCL's build-time sequence'), so the draw comes from SBCL's build-time *random-state*. Worse, the shipped node is built by scripts/build-node-core.lisp, which does (asdf:load-system "bitcoin-lisp") and then sb-ext:save-lisp-and-die - so the value is frozen into the executable's heap and is identical in every run of that binary. %evict-keyed-netgroup then computes (sxhash (cons *eviction-netgroup-secret* group)), which is a plain deterministic SBCL hash, not a keyed PRF.
findings.impact: The +evict-protect-netgroup+ pass (4 protected inbound slots, eviction.lisp:56-58, whose own docstring says 'an attacker cannot tell which netgroups will be protected without the node's key') is fully computable offline by anyone holding the binary, and the repository is public so the build is reproducible. An attacker enumerates candidate netgroups, computes (sxhash (cons SECRET group)) for each, connects from the four that sort highest, and those connections can never be selected by evict-least-valuable-inbound. That is the inbound half of eclipse resistance defeated by a predictable secret. Same class as Core's stated reason for keying the netgroup at all.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval in the project container. (1) Read the live value twice across a full image restart: 1717150972126639700 then 2578178878741551465, with bitcoin-lisp::*random-state-seed* = NIL both times, proving the global RNG is NOT re-seeded during system load and the draw comes from the build-time state. (2) Confirmed SBCL 2.6.5's build-time state is a process constant: three fresh `sbcl --no-userinit --no-sysinit` children each printed (113500 2499109626526694126) for (list (random 1000000) (random most-positive-fixnum)). (3) Positive control for the save-lisp-and-die freeze: built a child core with (defvar *s* (random most-positive-fixnum)) followed by sb-ext:save-lisp-and-die :executable t, then ran the produced executable three times - 1193941380623146742 every time. That is exactly the shape of scripts/build-node-core.lisp.

findings.title: VERSION user agent has neither Core's 256-byte cap nor SanitizeString, so a peer forges debug.log lines
findings.our_ref: src/serialization/message-macro.lisp:114-116 (the :var-string codec row), src/serialization/messages.lisp:204 (user-agent field), src/networking/peer.lisp:1115-1116 (stored raw), src/node/listen.lisp:44-47 and src/node/peers.lisp:569 (logged raw), src/rpc/net.lisp:240 (getpeerinfo "subver"), src/logging.lisp:100-115 (%log-escape-message passes newline through, like Core's LogEscapeMessage)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/net.h:67 (MAX_SUBVERSION_LENGTH = 256); refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:3640-3641 (vRecv >> LIMITED_STRING(strSubVer, MAX_SUBVERSION_LENGTH); cleanSubVer = SanitizeString(strSubVer)); refs/bitcoin/src/util/strencodings.cpp:30-39 (SanitizeString); refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:761,821,828 and net_processing.cpp:3582,3817,4017,5167,5284,5286 (every log line that prints a peer-supplied message type wraps it in SanitizeString)
findings.core_does: Core deserializes subVer through LIMITED_STRING, which THROWS ('String length limit exceeded') above 256 bytes, then stores only SanitizeString(strSubVer) - characters outside SAFE_CHARS_DEFAULT, newline included, are dropped before the string ever reaches a log line or getpeerinfo. Core applies SanitizeString at the boundary and LogEscapeMessage at the log; LogEscapeMessage deliberately lets newline through, so the first layer is what stops log-line forgery.
findings.we_do: The generated read-version-message reads the user agent with (map 'string #'code-char (br-read-var-bytes br)) - bounded only by +max-message-payload+ (4,000,000, config.lisp:298) - and stores it verbatim on the peer. There is no SanitizeString equivalent anywhere in src/ (grep for 'sanitize' finds only miniscript's ms-sanitize-type). The raw string is written to debug.log at handshake and returned as getpeerinfo's "subver".
findings.impact: A remote, unauthenticated peer controls up to ~4 MB of arbitrary bytes per connection in debug.log and in every getpeerinfo response (125 inbound slots = ~500 MB of user-agent strings held and re-serialized on each call). Embedding 0x0A produces additional, well-formed-looking debug.log lines: a monitor or an assert_debug_log-style scraper reads an attacker-written 'Shutdown: done'. ANSI escapes are neutralised by %log-escape-message, the newline is not - which is correct behaviour copied from Core, minus the SanitizeString layer that makes it safe there.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: built a version-message whose user agent is "/Satoshi:27.0/" + LF + "FORGED" + 200,000 'A's, wrote it with the generated write-version-message and read it back with read-version-message. Result (:PAYLOAD-BYTES 200111 :UA-LEN 200021 :IDENTICAL T :MAX-PAYLOAD 4000000) - no cap, no filtering, byte-identical round trip. Then fed a user agent containing LF + "2026-09-05 FORGED Shutdown: done" + ESC[31m through bitcoin-lisp.logging::format-log-entry: (:NEWLINE-PASSES-THROUGH T :ESC-WAS-ESCAPED T :LINES 2), and the rendered entry is two lines, the second being the attacker's.

findings.title: -blocknotify fires on every connected block including IBD and reindex
findings.our_ref: src/node/notify.lisp:20-28 (the :updated-block-tip hook), src/validation/block.lisp:2835 (notify-updated-block-tip fires after EVERY connect-block), src/validation/block.lisp:4016 (and after every activation step), src/logging.lisp:567-586 (run-notify-command -> uiop:launch-program, detached)
findings.core_does: Core connects -blocknotify to NotifyBlockTip and the very first line of the handler is `if (sync_state != SynchronizationState::POST_INIT) return;` - the command is suppressed for every tip update during initial block download and reindex, and only runs once the node is past init.
findings.we_do: notify-block-tip has only one guard, (not (chain-state-target-blockhash chainstate)), which excludes an assumeutxo background chainstate. There is no POST_INIT / IBD gate, and notify-updated-block-tip is announced after every single connected block, not per activation batch.
findings.impact: An operator who configures -blocknotify (a standard Core setup for block explorers, mining and monitoring) and then syncs from scratch, reindexes, or restores from a snapshot forks one detached /bin/sh per connected block - hundreds of thousands of processes as fast as blocks connect. On a mainnet sync that is a self-inflicted fork bomb; even on testnet4 it is tens of thousands of spawns. Core's gate exists precisely to prevent this. Secondary effect: every one of those invocations is a spurious 'new best block' signal to whatever the hook drives.
findings.executed: No: read-only. Both call sites were located by grep (only flush.lisp, notify.lisp and housekeeping.lisp subscribe to :updated-block-tip, and only notify.lisp runs a shell command) and the Core gate was read at init.cpp:2012. Reproducing it needs a syncing node with -blocknotify set, which I did not run.

findings.title: txospenderindex has no startup rewind, so a marker off the active chain leaves abandoned-branch spenders
findings.our_ref: src/node/indexes.lisp:89-115 (catch-up-index), src/node/indexes.lisp:22-50 (index-prepare-sync methods exist for blockfilterindex and coinstatsindex ONLY), src/storage/index-base.lisp:115-121 (the default index-prepare-sync is a no-op), src/storage/txospenderindex.lisp:55-57 (index-height ignores the chainstate and returns the stored height), src/storage/txospenderindex.lisp:64-71
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/index/base.cpp:200-247 (BaseIndex::Sync calls Rewind(pindex, pindex_next->pprev) whenever the stored best block is not the parent of the next block to index); refs/bitcoin/src/index/base.cpp:289-300 (Rewind -> CustomRemove per disconnected block); refs/bitcoin/src/index/txospenderindex.cpp:74-77 (options.disconnect_data = true) and :136 (CustomRemove)
findings.core_does: Core's TxoSpenderIndex opts into disconnect data and implements CustomRemove, and BaseIndex::Sync detects at every startup that the stored best block is not on the active chain and rewinds the index to the fork point, erasing the entries the abandoned branch wrote.
findings.we_do: catch-up-index calls index-prepare-sync, but txospender-index inherits the base no-op; its index-height declares (declare (ignore chainstate)) and returns the raw stored height, so a marker naming a block on an abandoned branch is never detected. If that height is at or above the tip, (when (< (index-height index cs) tip) ...) is false and no backfill runs either. index-rewind-block is reached only through the live :block-disconnected hook, which cannot fire for blocks that were disconnected while the process was not running.
findings.impact: After a crash (or kill) that leaves the index ahead of the last flushed chainstate, or after any restart onto a different branch, the spender index keeps outpoint -> spender entries for transactions that are no longer on the chain. gettxspendingprevout and anything else built on -txospenderindex then report an output as spent by a transaction that is not in the active chain. Bounded: the index is opt-in (default off), the connect hook moves the marker back on the next connected block, and the stale rows are only wrong for outputs whose real spender never re-appears. The coinstatsindex and blockfilterindex both have the repair this one lacks (indexes.lisp:22 and :47), which is what makes the gap look like an omission rather than a decision.
findings.executed: No: read-only, on both trees. I did not build the crash-then-reorg matrix; that is the crash-consistency lane the GA10 critic asks for. GA11's storage/second-reader dimension inherits the reproduction.

findings.title: P2P nonces, addrman selection and relay jitter all draw from one MT19937 stream where Core uses FastRandomContext
findings.our_ref: src/node/entropy.lisp:33-61 (seed-global-random-state installs one sb-ext:seed-random-state into the global CL:*RANDOM-STATE*), and the consumers: src/serialization/messages.lisp:333 (VERSION nonce), :348 (ping nonce), :624/:648 (compact-block nonce), src/networking/peer.lisp:848 (sendtxrcncl salt), :1329/:1346/:1395/:1435, src/networking/addrman.lisp:425,508,520,521,527,532,575,595 (new/tried bucket + position selection, acceptance probability, GetAddr shuffle), src/networking/protocol.lisp:1100,2630,2871,3205 (addr-relay reservoir, response-cache jitter, Poisson timers, initial-broadcast jitter), src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1535 (mempool.dat obfuscation key)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/random.h (FastRandomContext, ChaCha20-backed, OS-seeded); refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp (PeerManagerImpl::m_rng, deterministic only under the test-only option); refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:3369-3379 + init.cpp:1642 (per-process nSeed0/nSeed1); refs/bitcoin/src/addrman.cpp (AddrManImpl::insecure_rand, a FastRandomContext)
findings.core_does: Every draw listed above comes from a ChaCha20-based FastRandomContext seeded from the OS. Observing any number of Core's ping or version nonces tells an attacker nothing about the next addrman selection, addr-relay timer or feeler decision, because the generator is cryptographic.
findings.we_do: One process-global CL:*RANDOM-STATE* - SBCL's MT19937 - is seeded once with 256 bits of OS entropy at init-node and is then the single source for both the values we PUBLISH on the wire (VERSION nonce, ping nonces, sendtxrcncl salt, compact-block nonces) and the values we must keep SECRET (which addrman address is dialled next, addr-relay reservoir choice and Poisson timers, feeler cadence, the 1-in-3 tie-breaks). The addrman bucket KEY itself is fine - make-addrman-key reads /dev/urandom (addrman.lisp:40-49) - so this is about selection and timing, not bucket placement.
findings.impact: MT19937 is not a CSPRNG: its 19937-bit state is recoverable in closed form from 624 consecutive tempered 32-bit outputs, and it can be run backwards as well as forwards. Our published 64-bit nonces are drawn from the same stream as everything above, so a peer that collects enough of them (one long-lived connection's pings, or a few hundred short connections) can reconstruct the state and then predict which addrman address we dial next, when we relay addresses, and when we open a feeler - the inputs an eclipse attacker wants. I did NOT implement the state-recovery step, so this is the mechanism plus a well-known property of the generator, not an end-to-end exploit.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: bound *random-state* to a fixed seed and showed that consuming 0, 1 or 2 (random (expt 2 64)) nonces shifts the subsequent addrman-shaped draws - (482 37 0.6327...) / (285 1 0.3678...) / (420 41 0.4091...) - and that replaying the same seed reproduces the first triple exactly. That proves the wire nonces and the addrman/relay draws are one and the same stream and are a deterministic function of its state.

findings.title: define-message :var-string is Latin-1, not bytes: a wallet label above U+00FF is a TYPE-ERROR
findings.our_ref: src/serialization/message-macro.lisp:114-116, src/wallet/wallet-store.lisp:96 and :340 (define-wdb-value string), src/wallet/wallet.lisp:664-680 (wallet-set-address-book writes the label through wdb-string-value), src/wallet/wallet.lisp:1104-1107 (read back), src/rpc/server.lisp:1090 (hunchentoot raw-post-data :force-text t decodes the JSON body as UTF-8)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/serialize.h (std::string is serialized as its raw bytes, with no character decoding); refs/bitcoin/src/wallet/walletdb.cpp (address-book 'name' records hold the label's bytes verbatim)
findings.core_does: Core stores and transports a string as the bytes it received; a UTF-8 label is written and read back unchanged, whatever code points it contains.
findings.we_do: The one codec row shared by define-message and the wallet's define-wdb-key / define-wdb-value maps bytes to characters with CODE-CHAR and back with CHAR-CODE - i.e. Latin-1, not bytes. Any character above U+00FF cannot be written at all (the CHAR-CODE result does not fit the (unsigned-byte 8) result vector), and a byte sequence that is really UTF-8 comes back as one character per byte.
findings.impact: The RPC layer decodes the request body as UTF-8, so `setlabel`/`getnewaddress` with a label containing any non-Latin-1 character (all CJK, Cyrillic, emoji) reaches wallet-set-address-book as a string with code points above 255 and the wallet store raises a raw TYPE-ERROR instead of storing the label. Latin-1 labels do survive our own round trip, so the practical effect is a hard, badly reported failure for non-Latin-1 labels rather than data corruption. Descriptors and addresses are ASCII, so they are unaffected; the P2P user agent is unaffected in the outbound direction because -uacomment is already sanitized (config/values.lisp:147-156).
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: (bitcoin-lisp.wallet::wdb-string-value "hi") -> #(2 104 105); with (code-char 233) -> #(1 233), i.e. one Latin-1 byte where Core would write the two UTF-8 bytes C3 A9; with (code-char 20013) -> TYPE-ERROR. Reading Core-shaped UTF-8 back, (wdb-parse-string-value #(2 195 169)) -> the two-character string "A~(c)" rather than "e-acute".

findings.title: A boolean wire field is true only for the byte 1; Core treats every nonzero byte as true
findings.our_ref: src/serialization/message-macro.lisp:109 (the :bool codec row), src/serialization/messages.lisp:206-210 (the version message's relay flag repeats the same (= ... 1) test in its :read form), src/serialization/messages.lisp:604-610 (parse-sendcmpct-payload)
findings.core_ref: refs/bitcoin/src/serialize.h:277 (`template <typename Stream> void Unserialize(Stream& s, bool& a) { uint8_t f = ser_readdata8(s); a = f; }`); refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:3647 and :3684-3705 (vRecv >> fRelay); refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:3907-3922 (vRecv >> sendcmpct_hb)
findings.core_does: Core's bool unserializer assigns the raw byte to a bool, so any nonzero value is true. A peer sending fRelay = 2 is a peer that wants transaction announcements, and sendcmpct with announce = 2 selects us as its high-bandwidth peer.
findings.we_do: Both the generated :bool reader and the two hand-written readers that repeat the pattern test (= byte 1), so every nonzero byte other than 1 reads as FALSE.
findings.impact: A peer whose VERSION carries fRelay = 2 is recorded as not wanting transactions and never receives our inv announcements, where Core would relay to it; a sendcmpct with announce = 2 does not put us in high-bandwidth mode. Narrow in practice - Core itself only ever writes 0 or 1 - but it is a divergence in how we read another implementation's wire bytes, and the generated :bool row would spread it to any future field that uses it. Distinct from the GA10 finding 98069fe2 (sendcmpct(0) not clearing the high-bandwidth-from flag), which is about the 0 case.
findings.executed: scripts/dev.sh eval: serialized a version message, set its last byte (the relay flag) to 2 and read it back - version-message-relay is NIL. parse-sendcmpct-payload on #(2 2 0 0 0 0 0 0 0) returns (NIL 2), i.e. announce = false for an announce byte of 2.

coverage_note: Read in full and executed against: src/node/{indexes,state,entropy,sync,listen,notify,housekeeping,wallet-hooks,mempool-persist,reindex,params}.lisp, src/rpc/accessors.lisp, src/serialization/message-macro.lisp, src/coalton/{serialization,binary,types,crypto}.lisp, src/networking/fd-wait.lisp, src/util/ratelimit.lisp, src/storage/coins-view-migration.lisp, plus src/storage/{index-base,txindex,txospenderindex}.lisp and src/node/eviction.lisp as the drive/consumer sites the named files reach. Container up throughout (bitcoin-lisp-sbcl:2.6.5-4); five of the seven findings were reached by running code. CLEARED, no finding: fd-wait.lisp - sb-unix:unix-simple-poll was probed on a live pipe and returns T on POLLHUP (so EOF is seen), NIL on POLLNVAL and NIL for a bogus fd, and every caller passes an explicit numeric timeout, so the latent (:timeout nil -> 0 ms) divergence is unreachable; ratelimit.lisp - the 'one bucket, one thread' claim holds by call graph (per-peer buckets are touched only from check-peer-rate-limit on the sync thread) and the RPC bucket is in fact lock-guarded at rpc/server.lisp:701-716, so the file comment understates rather than overstates the safety; message-macro.lisp header codec - the generated writer produces Core's canonical mainnet verack byte for byte (f9beb4d9 76657261636b000000000000 00000000 5df6e0e2); listen.lisp - the serial-accept slow-loris shape is already bounded (15 s per step, %await-verack has an absolute budget with a documented history, and inbound-connection-allowed-p bounds the hand-off queue), and the residual is the already-reported 'inbound handshake inline on accept thread' on the exclusion list; the -prune incompatibilities with -txindex, -txospenderindex and -reindex-chainstate are all present (init.lisp:292-306) and match init.cpp:1002-1009; housekeeping.lisp's CheckDiskSpace floor is Core's 52428800 and the df field index is right; %account-message already folds unknown message types into a shared bucket, so the GA1-9 accounting finding is fixed. NOT COVERED, and who inherits it: (1) the crash-consistency matrix the coinstatsindex header describes - I reasoned about kill-9 windows but ran no kill-then-restart, so the coinstatsindex rewind and the txospenderindex gap above are both unreproduced; GA11 dimension 9 (second reader: validation/block.lisp + chain.lisp + coins-view-cache.lisp) inherits it. (2) The full node-lock discipline audit: I checked the four documented rules against the waitfor* RPCs, the ban/scan/gbt/txoutset leaf locks and the listener, and found no cycle, but I did not enumerate all 140 node-lock sites nor every mutating RPC; note that accessors.lisp's leaf-lock list names five locks while the tree has at least twelve (*gbt-cache-lock*, *txoutset-scan-lock*, *scanblocks-lock*, *compact-block-metrics-lock*, *outbound-protection-lock*, *outbound-nonce-lock*, *peer-id-lock*, *rpc-rate-limiter-lock*) - GA11 dimension 10 (protocol.lisp + peer.lisp) and dimension 8 (rpc) inherit the rest. (3) src/coalton/{serialization,binary,types}.lisp are DEAD outside tests - no file under src/ except src/coalton/package.lisp names bl.cser or bl.cbin, and bitcoin-lisp.coalton.script imports only from coalton.crypto - so their missing BIP144 support, missing non-canonical-CompactSize check and unbounded read-bytes are not reachable from the network; I recorded no finding for them, and dimension 12's successor (script interpreter) should decide whether to delete them. crypto.lisp IS on the consensus path (OP_HASH160/HASH256/SHA256/RIPEMD160, script.lisp:1404-1434 and :2448) and I found nothing wrong with it. (4) mempool-persist.lisp: our LoadMempool has no expiry filter where Core's mempool_persist.cpp:100 skips entries older than pool.m_opts.expiry and counts them 'expired', and it does not distinguish Core's 'already there' bucket - both are acknowledged in our own docstring and bounded to one block interval, so I filed neither; the mempool.dat byte format itself (read-core-mempool-file-bytes) belongs to the mempool dimension. (5) reindex.lisp rebuilds the UTXO set from stored blocks with no script re-validation, which its docstring states as a deliberate choice - not filed. (6) src/node/logging.lisp, src/rpc/output-script.lisp, src/util/context.lisp, src/util/conditions.lisp, src/wallet/signmessage.lisp and src/networking/{minisketch,txreconciliation-set}.lisp are on the critic's never-opened list but were outside my assignment; dimension 8 (rpc/util) inherits output-script.lisp.
